title: C++ Foundations & OOPs
tagline: MAANG-grade — memory internals, polymorphism machinery, design under O(1) contracts

placementQuiz.q: Deleting a derived object through a base pointer WITHOUT virtual destructor…
options: base dtor runs only → derived resources leak
placementQuiz.explain: Static binding picks Base::~Base; derived's cleanup never happens.

placementQuiz.q: Where does `new int[100]` live? Where does the pointer itself live?
placementQuiz.explain: Pointer variable is a local (stack); the array block is heap.

options: exclusive ownership vs reference-counted shared ownership
placementQuiz.explain: unique = single owner, zero overhead; shared = many owners + control block counting.

placementQuiz.q: std::vector push_back worst case is O(n) yet we call it amortized O(1) because…
options: doubling makes total cost of k pushes O(k) → constant average
placementQuiz.explain: Geometric growth spreads copy costs across all prior pushes.

placementQuiz.q: LRU Cache gets O(1) get AND put via…
placementQuiz.explain: Map answers 'where', DLL reorders in O(1) by splicing nodes.

sections.title: Mental model — the program's memory map

blocks.md: At MAANG level, "a box in memory" becomes **which region owns that box**. Every running program splits memory into segments with different lifetimes and rules — leaks, crashes and interview follow-ups all live in these boundaries.

segments.name: Heap
segments.desc: `new` allocations — grows up, YOU manage lifetime

segments.name: Stack
segments.desc: locals + call frames — grows down, auto-cleans

blocks.md: **Stack cleans itself (scope-bound). Heap never cleans itself — someone must own every `new`. Ownership is THE design question.**

blocks.label: where does each thing live
blocks.py:
# Python memory model hides segments, but the MENTAL map still applies:
g = 10                    # module-level ~ 'data segment'

def demo():
    local = [1, 2]        # list OBJECT lives on heap; name in frame
    p = {'k': 42}         # dicts likewise heap-backed
    del local             # refcount drops; GC reclaims (no manual free)
# Lesson: ownership anxiety disappears, but SHARED-MUTABLE traps remain
# (same dict passed around = same object everywhere).

blocks.md: **The four heap sins:** leak (no delete) · double-delete · use-after-free (dangling) · forgetting `delete[]` for arrays. Each has ended interviews at the follow-up stage.

items.q: Function returns `int* f(){ int x=5; return &x; }` — bug?
options: returns dangling pointer — stack frame died at return
items.explain: Address outlives its storage; dereferencing is undefined behavior.
Array form pairs with delete[] so element destructors run correctly.

items.q: Two million tiny `new`s in a loop mainly cause…
options: fragmentation + slow allocs — batch into containers instead
items.explain: Heap bookkeeping per-allocation is expensive; prefer owning containers.

blocks.md: **virtual = decide at RUNTIME by looking at the object's actual type (via its vtable). Non-virtual = decided at COMPILE time by the pointer's declared type.**

Each polymorphic class carries one hidden **vtable** (array of function pointers). Each object carries one hidden **vptr** to it. Calling a virtual function means: fetch vptr → index slot → jump. One indirection buys runtime flexibility — that's the whole cost model interviewers want you to articulate.

blocks.label: the classic trap, then fix

blocks.title: Trace: `delete b` with and without virtual dtor
steps: runtime: vptr says actual type Derived

chain.q: Why can't C++ have virtual constructors?
chain.a: Virtual dispatch needs an EXISTING object's vptr to consult; a constructor's job is creating the object — nothing to dispatch on yet. Factory functions (clone()/create()) are the idiom replacing it.
One vptr per object (8 bytes typical), one indirection per call, blocks some inlining. Fine at API boundaries; hot inner loops avoid it.

chain.q: When is a protected non-virtual destructor correct?
chain.a: Policy classes/base-for-CRTP where deletion through base pointer is forbidden by design — deleting is prevented at compile time instead of made polymorphic.

items.explain: Every instance carries its own vptr pointing at its class's shared vtable.

items.q: Constructor bodies run during virtual calls as…
options: the object is PARTIAL — virtual dispatch behaves like the current class under construction
items.explain: During Base() construction the vptr still points at Base — calling pure virtuals there crashes/UB.

sections.title: Ownership engineering — RAII, smart pointers, moves

blocks.md: **RAII: wrap resource lifetime in object lifetime. Constructor acquires, destructor releases — then scope IS your cleanup, even during exceptions.**

blocks.label: smart pointers replace manual new/delete
blocks.py:
# No smart pointers needed - reference counting + cycle GC handle it.
# Weak references exist for observer/cycle cases:
import weakref
cache = weakref.WeakValueDictionary()   # entries vanish when objects die
# unique_ptr discipline  -> single owner variable, nobody else aliases
# shared_ptr discipline  -> many names fine; cycles break via weakref

rows.label: When you write ONE of dtor/copy-ctor/copy-assign…
rows.right: …and consider move ctor + move assign too

rows.label: Best practice
rows.right: ZERO of them: hold unique_ptr/vector members and defaults are correct

rows.label: Move semantics
rows.right: steal the resource from expiring objects (std::move)

blocks.label: move = steal the guts
blocks.py:
# Python assignment IS move-like: names are references, never copies
b = a                       # both names point at same object (O(1))
import copy
c = copy.deepcopy(a)        # that's what a real 'copy' costs
# std::move has no analogue because there is nothing to steal -
# rebinding a name transfers the reference instantly.

blocks.md: **Interview soundbite:** *"Copy duplicates the resource; move transfers ownership in O(1). std::move doesn't move — it casts to rvalue, PERMISSION to move."*

items.q: Exception thrown after `new` but before `delete` in raw code causes…
options: LEAK — stack unwinds skipping delete line
items.explain: RAII fixes this class of bug structurally, not vigilantly.

items.q: Two objects holding shared_ptr to EACH OTHER will…
options: never free — reference counts never reach zero (cycle)
items.explain: Classic cycle leak; one side becomes weak_ptr (non-owning observer).

options: no — it leaves b1 valid-but-unspecified (usually empty)

blocks.md: L2 showed vector doubling. The formal tool: **aggregate cost over a sequence ÷ operations**. Geometric growth ⇒ total O(n) for n ops ⇒ amortized O(1). Interviewers test whether you can PROVE it, not recite it.

blocks.label: MinStack — pattern: carry derived state

chain.a: Encode deltas: push 2x−min when x<min (recover old min = 2·encoded−x on pop). Great follow-up theatre; say trade-off aloud: time unchanged, space halved-ish, readability destroyed.
vector + unordered_map(value→indices). Delete = swap element with last, pop_back, update map — swap-to-end is THE O(1)-delete-from-array idiom (LC 380).

chain.q: Why must LRU use DOUBLY linked list (not singly)?
chain.a: Need to unlink a node given only that node — requires O(1) access to prev. Singly forces O(n) predecessor hunt.

blocks.title: Trace: LC380 delete via swap-to-end (set={4,8,2}, delete 8)

options: range [L,R] huge but R−L+1 small — sieve ONLY that window using base primes ≤√R
items.explain: Memory follows window size, not R itself — decomposition thinking reused everywhere.

items.q: unordered_map worst-case lookup degrades to O(n) when…
options: all keys collide in one bucket (adversarial hashing)
items.explain: Know the worst case even while quoting the average — MAANG loves this distinction.

sections.title: Problem set — L3 hard with interviewer follow-up chains

items.title: Reverse Integer (overflow-proof)
items.statement: Reverse digits; return 0 on 32-bit overflow — WITHOUT using 64-bit blindly (defend your check).
hints: Check BEFORE multiplying: rev > INT_MAX/10, or == and digit>7.
Negative bound differs by 1 (−2147483648) — asymmetric limits.
Say WHY pop/push framing makes the inequality valid.

items.title: Copy List with Random Pointer
items.statement: Deep-copy a list where each node also points randomly. O(1) space solution exists.
hints: Map approach: original→clone dict, two passes.
O(1) space: interleave clones A→A'→B→B'… , split random links, then unweave.
This IS your shallow-vs-deep lesson weaponized.

items.title: Design HashMap
items.statement: Implement put/get/remove with array-of-buckets + chaining; discuss load factor & resize.
hints: Fixed bucket array; index = key % size.
Chaining via vector<pair<..>> per bucket.
Follow-up bait: why prime-ish size? what breaks at load factor >1?

items.title: Min Stack
items.statement: All four ops O(1). Then defend the pair-stored-min against the delta-encoding variant.
hints: Store (value, minSoFar) pairs.
Alternative: encoded-deltas stack for space-flex trade-off.
Interviewer wants trade-off narration, not just code.

items.title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
items.statement: Average O(1) insert, remove, getRandom (uniform). The swap-to-end idiom is the whole game.
hints: vector stores values; map value→index.
Delete: overwrite with back(), pop_back(), patch map.
getRandom: rand() % size.

items.title: Segmented Sieve [L, R]
items.statement: Print primes in [L,R] where R ≤ 10⁹ but R−L+1 ≤ 10⁶.
hints: Sieve base primes up to √R first (≈31623).
Window boolean array indexed offset = pos − L.
Mark multiples of each base prime starting max(p², ceil(L/p)*p).

items.title: Closest Prime Numbers in Range
items.statement: Return the closest prime PAIR inside [left,right] — compose segmentation + linear scan.
hints: Build window primes via segmented sieve.
Scan consecutive primes tracking minimal gap.
Early exit impossible in general — justify complexity.

items.title: LRU Cache
items.statement: get & put in O(1) with capacity eviction. Then explain why every alternative fails.
hints: unordered_map<key, Node*> + DLL ordered by recency.
Head = MRU, tail = LRU; splice on touch.
Kill alternatives: array (O(n) reorder), singly-list (O(n) unlink), heap (O(log n))

items.title: Virtual Destructor Leak Demo
items.statement: Write Base/Derived owning heap arrays; prove the leak WITHOUT virtual, fix it, then explain vptr mechanics.
hints: Run both versions watching process memory or sanitizer output.
Explain static vs dynamic dispatch sentence-by-sentence.
Extend: protected dtor variant for policy bases.

revisionCard: Memory map: Text/Data-BSS/Heap/Stack — ownership question decides correctness
Four heap sins: leak · double-delete · use-after-free · wrong delete form
virtual = runtime vtable dispatch; virtual dtor REQUIRED for delete-through-base
RAII: scope = cleanup; smart pointers encode ownership (unique exclusive / shared counted / weak observer)
Move = O(1) ownership transfer; std::move is permission, not action
Amortized proof = total(sequence)/ops; geometric growth ⇒ O(1) avg
Design idioms: aux-state travels with data (MinStack) · swap-to-end delete (LC380) · dll+map (LRU)

Resource Acquisition Is Initialization — acquire in ctor, release in dtor.
Valid-but-unspecified object state after being stolen from; assignable/destroyable only.
Non-owning observer breaking shared_ptr cycles; locks to temp shared on use.
